`starsim_data` gives you national demographic data, age-structured contact matrices and subnational administrative boundaries, ready to use in a disease model. This page walks through the main functions in the order you are likely to need them. None of the examples need an internet connection.

## Installation

::: {.panel-tabset}

## pip

```bash
pip install starsim_data
```

## with spatial support

```bash
pip install "starsim_data[spatial]"
```

## from a clone

```bash
git clone https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data
pip install -e starsim_data
```

:::

The package includes about 9 MB of data. The `[spatial]` option also installs `geopandas`, `pyogrio` and `rastertoolkit`, which you only need for the boundary shapes and population maps described in [Spatial data](user-guide/spatial.qmd).

## Listing what is available

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True)[['dataset', 'description', 'access', 'locations']]
```

The `access` column says how you get each dataset. **Bundled** data is inside the package and loads instantly, with no internet connection. **Fetched** data is prepared by this package but kept out of it to save space; it is downloaded from this package's own releases the first time you use it. **Downloaded** data comes from its original publisher, such as the UN. Both fetched and downloaded data are saved on your computer after the first use. [Bundled, fetched and downloaded data](user-guide/access.qmd) explains the difference.

## Loading a dataset

```{python}
deaths = ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths')
deaths.head()
```

The result is a `sciris.dataframe`, which is a kind of `pandas.DataFrame`, so everything you do with pandas works. The column names are the UN's own: `Time`, `Sex`, `AgeGrpStart` and `mx` are the names used in World Population Prospects, and also the names Starsim's demographic modules expect.

Contact matrices are square, with rows and columns labeled by the start age of each age group:

```{python}
matrix = ssd.load('kenya', which='prem2021')
matrix.iloc[:5, :5]
```

So you can pick out values by age:

```{python}
matrix.loc[25, 30]   # daily contacts between the 25-29 and 30-34 bins
```

## Specifying locations

You don't need to know the exact name the package uses. ISO codes, official names, common abbreviations, and French, Spanish or Portuguese names are all recognized, and accents, case and punctuation are ignored.

```{python}
[ssd.resolve(name) for name in
 ['USA', 'US', 'united states', 'United States of America', 'Etats-Unis']]
```

```{python}
[ssd.resolve(name) for name in ["Côte d'Ivoire", 'cote divoire', 'Ivory Coast', 'CIV']]
```

A name that doesn't match gives an error rather than a guess, though the error suggests what you might have meant: `ssd.load('Keyna', which='deaths')` gives "location 'Keyna' not found (did you mean: Kenya, China, Ghana?)". [Locations](user-guide/locations.qmd) has more on which names are recognized.

## Inspecting the data visually

Plotting the data before you use it is an easy way to catch the wrong country or a units mistake.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: 100%
ssd.plot('kenya');
```

The summary figure shows the age pyramid, the crude birth rate over time, mortality by age and sex, and the contact matrix. Use `which=` to draw one panel on its own.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 100%
ssd.plot('kenya', which='deaths', year=2050);
```

## Attribution

Each dataset records its source, license and citation, so you know what to cite:

```{python}
prov = ssd.provenance('prem2021')
{k: prov[k] for k in ['source', 'license', 'citation']}
```

The same information is attached to every frame returned by `load()`:

```{python}
deaths.attrs['provenance'].license
```

[Provenance and reproducibility](user-guide/provenance.qmd) has more on this.

## Subnational geography

Subnational geography is bundled too, as a table of administrative units (provinces, states, districts and so on) with their locations, areas and populations:

```{python}
nodes = ssd.load_nodes('kenya', level=1)
nodes.head()
```

```{python}
ssd.distances('kenya', level=1).iloc[:4, :4].round(1)
```

Center points, areas and the distances between units need no extra packages and no downloads. Boundary shapes, for drawing maps, are an optional extra described in [Spatial data](user-guide/spatial.qmd).

## Data that is not bundled

The bundled demographic data gives one year per decade, from the UN's Medium projection variant. For every year, complete life tables, or other projection variants, use `download()`, which gets the data from the UN the first time and saves it on your computer:

```python
ssd.download('kenya', which='deaths', years=(2000, 2025))  # annual rather than decadal
ssd.download('kenya', which='life_table', years=2020)      # qx, lx, ex, and the rest
ssd.download('kenya', which='births', variant='High')      # a different projection variant
```

[Bundled, fetched and downloaded data](user-guide/access.qmd) explains the difference, and is a good page to read next.
